title: Six years
hookLine: years of hard austerity; some think he has died

cards: Brave, or just stubborn? From inside a long, hard stretch, a degree that takes years, a job that can't be left, caring for someone who is ill, the two can look exactly the same. So can pushing on and being stuck.
Tradition says the wanderer spent six years this way, in the forests near Uruvela. Breathless meditation. Fasting.
Standing instead of sitting. Lying on a bed of thorns, by his own later account. His five companions watching, waiting.
And in the later telling, one day he collapses.

teach.b: In the Buddha's own account, there's a strange moment. When some gods saw him, they said, the wanderer Gotama is dead. Others said, he's not dead, but he's dying.
Others said, he's neither: this is simply how an awakened one lives. Nobody could tell. The later telling makes it vivid.
He faints while walking and falls to the ground, and a god runs to his father, King Suddhodana: your son is dead. The old king, who had tried so hard to keep him in the palace, refuses to believe it.

teach.h: MY SON WILL NOT DIE YET.
teach.b: My son will not die, he says, before he reaches what he went looking for. Six years. The Buddha's own account gives no number; the six years come from later tradition.
But the length is the point. This wasn't a weekend. It was years of a life, given completely to one method.
And the Buddha's verdict, looking back, is calm and devastating.

teach.h: NO ASCETIC HAD FELT MORE PAIN.
teach.b: Whatever painful feelings any ascetic has ever felt, past, present or future, this was the utmost. There's none beyond it. And still, it didn't lead to awakening.
The Buddha isn't against effort. He'll later make right effort part of the path.
But effort pointed the wrong way only digs deeper into the wrong place.
A shovel works hard in a hole, too.

how: Buddhists speak of the six years of austerities as the extreme the Buddha tried and set aside, and teachers use them to warn against self-punishment in practice as well as against laziness.

o: the years he lived as a prince in the palace
the long stretch of austerities tradition gives him
the years he spent teaching after his awakening

games.q: what's inside the six years — tap the pairs.
p: refused to believe his son was dead

s: the Buddha's own account in MN 36 counts six years of austerity
MN 36 gives no number; the six years come from later tradition.
in the Buddha's account, some gods thought he was dead
others thought he was dying, and others that he was awake.
right effort is part of the path. he rejected effort pointed the wrong way.

games.q: you're King Suddhodana. a messenger runs in: your son has died in the forest. what do you say?
o: send soldiers to bring the body home.
my son will not die before he finds what he's looking for.
games.why: in the later telling, the old king refuses to believe it. and he's right: the wanderer had only fainted.

practice: Sit, or lie down if you can, notice where you're tired, the eyes, the back, the legs, the mind, and admit it gently to yourself: I'm tired here.
Don't fix it or push through it; on each out-breath, let that place get a little heavier, a little more supported by the chair or the floor. You're allowed to rest; the Buddha found out the hard way.

wordCard.voice: Six years. The time tradition gives to the wanderer's austerities: pain, he says, no ascetic had gone beyond, and still not the way.

orig.note: Pali (Sanskrit tapas): heat, austerity, the burning practice of self-denial the ascetics believed would purify.

carryVoice: Your line: harder isn't always better. Even the hard way has an end. Day forty-six, done.

sources.ref: Mahasaccaka Sutta (Majjhima Nikaya 36): the gods' views and the verdict on austerities
